## Job Market Paper


**Proximity to the Plague: Measuring Locust Exposure and Child Health** 

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>
I investigate the early childhood health outcomes of the Kenyan 2020--2021 desert locust invasion. To account for the multi harvest setting, I build a treatment that conditions on the insect's biological capacity to damage vegetation, the growth stage of the local crop, and subsequent vegetal decline, matching georeferenced locust observations to the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey. Children exposed in utero within 30~km of a verified damage event carry weight-for-height z-scores 0.185 standard deviations below the control group, and are 26 percent more likely to be clinically wasted. Height-for-age does not move. The estimate loads on third-trimester exposure. The effect is largest in riverine livelihood zones, where households depend most heavily on their own harvest and have the least market cushion when it fails: exposed riverine children lose an additional 0.25 standard deviations on weight-for-height beyond the average cropping-zone effect.
</details>

[PDF](./locust_kenya_sept_2025.pdf)

## Working Papers

**Wildfire smoke, air quality, and the limits of short-run labor-market impacts in Canadian cities**
*With [Christopher S. Cotton](https://christophercotton.ca/)* | Submitted August 2026: Nature Climate Change


<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>

Wildfire-smoke-driven increases in fine particulate matter raise hours worked and employment in Canada's nine largest metropolitan areas. This response is consistent with productivity impairment requiring longer hours to meet output targets and with degraded outdoor conditions reducing the value of non-work time. Both mechanisms imply welfare losses that standard labour-market statistics record as gains, suggesting output-based damage assessments understate the costs of smoke in urban economies. 

</details>

[PDF](./wildfire.pdf) | [Replication](https://github.com/zemarhakim/wildfire-smoke-labour-replication)


**Drought-Proof Generosity: Index Insurance and Informal Livestock Lending in Northern Kenya**
Last updated: April, 2026

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>

A central concern in the microinsurance literature is whether formal insurance contracts crowd out informal risk-sharing arrangements that underpin livelihoods in developing economies. Using six rounds of panel data from pastoralist households in Marsabit, northern Kenya, we estimate the causal effect of Index-Based Livestock Insurance (IBLI) on informal livestock lending during drought. We instrument IBLI uptake with randomly distributed price discount coupons and exploit exogenous variation in drought severity measured by the Standardised Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Our two-stage least squares estimates, corrected for small-cluster bias with 16 sub-location clusters, show that IBLI coverage significantly \emph{increases} the probability of borrowing livestock during drought---a crowding-in effect, not crowding out. A one-standard-deviation worsening of drought conditions raises the probability of livestock borrowing by roughly 39~percentage points more for insured than uninsured households. Placebo tests on livestock gifts and outward loans show no significant effects, supporting the exclusion restriction. Generalised random forest estimates reveal that treatment effect heterogeneity is driven primarily by drought severity and livestock wealth. These findings suggest that formal index insurance complements, rather than substitutes for, informal reciprocal lending networks, providing a new channel through which microinsurance improves household resilience.

</details>

[PDF](./ibli_kenya.pdf)


## Work in Progress


**Born into Drought: Early-Life Exposure and Child Health in Angola**
<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>
Observational estimates of drought's effect on child nutrition are 
likely severe underestimates: treatment is measured at geographic 
centroids that obscure the true variation in household-level water 
deficit. This paper estimates the causal effect of early-life drought 
exposure on stunting in Angola using a shift-share instrument that 
interacts atmospheric circulation with cluster-level rainfall 
sensitivity. The 2SLS estimate implies that a one-unit deterioration 
in a standard moisture index during the first year of life raises 
stunting prevalence by 35 percentage points. The first year is the 
critical exposure window in this sample, dominating birth-point and 
second-year specifications across all instrument and treatment 
combinations. These findings imply that the observational literature, 
which reports pooled estimates corresponding to roughly 3 percentage 
points in stunting prevalence per unit drought, understates the true 
nutritional cost of early-life moisture deficit by a factor of 
roughly twelve, with implications for the targeting and timing of 
pre-emptive nutrition and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions 
in drought-prone provinces of southern Africa.
</details>


## Policy Papers and Other Contributions


**Patent Monetization Promotion and SSO Participation**
*With Charles River Associates*
<details>
<summary>Project Details</summary>
Simcoe and Zhang (2021) study whether standard setting organizations' intellectual property rights (IPR) policies affect participation and innovation, using two natural experiments: the W3C's 2003 shift to royalty-free licensing and the IEEE's 2015 revision of its patent policy. Across both settings, they find little evidence that stricter IPR terms reduced participation by standard-essential patent (SEP) licensors or innovation in patent-intensive areas, though their IEEE analysis covers only a short post-revision window. This paper extends the IEEE portion of their study — working-group contributions, organization-level contributions, and CPC-level patent applications — through 2025. The organization-level result remains a precisely estimated null over the longer window. Two other results diverge from the original findings: 802.11's relative contribution growth becomes larger, other patent-intensive working groups now show a significant relative decline, and CPC groups more exposed to declared 802.11 patents show significantly higher post-2015 patenting. We argue these diverging results are more plausibly explained by the coincident Wi-Fi 6/6E and Wi-Fi 7 technology cycle than by the policy itself, and conclude that our extension does not overturn Simcoe and Zhang's (2021) central finding.
</details>

**G7 Sanctions Gap Analysis**
*With Global Affairs Canada* | Presented during Canada's G7 Presidency 
<details> 
<summary>Project Details</summary>
 This project compiled sanctions data for all five jurisdictions (US, UK, EU, Japan and Canada), recording for each affected product code and listing the specific legal citation (e.g., executive order, EU regulation article, or UK/Canada equivalent) authorizing the restriction, alongside indicators for whether the measure is an import restriction, export restriction, or listed persons. The resulting harmonized dataset allows for consistent measurement of the scope and overlap of allied sanctions regimes across countries. The report and associated analysis proivdes a foundation for measuring and understanding coordination (or divergence) toward Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the effectiveness of these measures in restricting bilateral trade flows.
</details>
